बिहार में बादलों की आवाजाही और छिटपुट वर्षा के बावजूद उमस बनी हुई है। मौसम विभाग ने अगले 24 घंटों ...और पढ़ें

बिहार में बादलों की आवाजाही के साथ उमस का प्रभाव।
पटना सहित 22 जिलों में अगले 24 घंटे वर्षा, वज्रपात की संभावना।
17 सितंबर को बेगूसराय, खगड़िया, मुजफ्फरपुर में भारी वर्षा का अलर्ट।
जागरण संवाददाता, पटना। बिहार में बादलों की आवाजाही बने होने के साथ कई स्थानों पर छिटपुट वर्षा के कारण उमस का प्रभाव बना हुआ है। मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र पटना के अनुसार, अगले 24 घंटे के दौरान राजधानी सहित 22 जिलों गया, औरंगाबाद, नालंदा, नवादा, शेखपुरा, लखीसराय, बेगूसराय, समस्तीपुर, वैशाली, मुजफ्फरपुर, सीतामढ़ी, शिवहर, मधुबनी, दरभंगा, सुपौल, अररिया, किशनंगज, पूर्णिया, कटिहार, लखीसराय, सहरसा , मधेपुरा में मेघ गर्जन, वज्रपात के साथ कई स्थानों पर छिटपुट वर्षा की संभावना है।
इन स्थानों पर हवा की गति 30-40 किमी प्रतिघंटा रहेगी। लखीसराय में 30 किमी प्रतिघंटा की रफ्तार से हवा दर्ज की गई। बीते 24 घंटे के दौरान प्रदेश के अलग-अलग भागों में वर्षा दर्ज की गई।
किशनगंज में सबसे ज्यादा बारिश
किशनगंज के गलगलिया में 75.4 मिमी सर्वाधिक वर्षा दर्ज की गई। सोमवार को पटना सहित आसपास इलाकों में बादलों की आवाजाही के साथ हल्की वर्षा से राहत मिलने के बाद उमस ने लोगों की परेशानी बढ़ाई।
सुबह 11 बजे के आसपास राजधानी में हल्की वर्षा के बाद धूप निकलने से उमस का प्रभाव बना रहा। सोमवार को गया को छोड़ कर पटना सहित शेष जिलों के अधिकतम तापमान में वृद्धि दर्ज की गई।
पटना का अधिकतम तापमान 34.7 डिग्री सेल्सियस एवं 38.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस के साथ भभुआ के कैमूर में सर्वाधिक तापमान दर्ज किया गया।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार उत्तर पश्चिम बंगाल की खाड़ी और इसके आसपास हवा का चक्रवाती परिसंचरण का क्षेत्र बने होने के कारण प्रदेश के कई भागों में बादलों की आवाजाही एवं कुछ स्थानों पर छिटपुट वर्षा से उमस का प्रभाव बने रहने की संभावना है। 17 सितंबर को बेगूसराय, खगड़िया, मुजफ्फरपुर एवं समस्तीपुर जिले के एक या दो स्थानों पर भारी वर्षा की संभावना है।

गोरखपुर में मंगलवार की सुबह से ही कभी धूप तो कभी बादल देखने को मिल रहा है। हल्की ठंडी हवाओं से गर्मी से काफी हद तक राहत है लेकिन नमी होने की वजह से उमस बरकरार है। जिससे लोगों को परेशानियों का सामना करना पड़ रहा है।
मौसम वैज्ञानिक कैलाश पांडेय के अनुसार आने वाले 3-4 दिनों तक मौसम ऐसा ही बनेगा रहेगा। कभी- कभी छिटपुट बारिश देखने को मिलेगी। उनका कहना है कि 18 सितंबर को शहर और आसपास के एरिया में गरज चमक के साथ अच्छी बारिश होने की संभावना है।
विभाग के आंकड़ों के मुताबिक इस महीने जिले में अबतक 43 मिमी बारिश हुई है। जबकि सितंबर में 221 मिमी औसत बारिश दर्ज की जाती है। आज शहर का अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 26 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने का अनुमान है।
कब होगी अच्छी बारिश मौसम वैज्ञानिक ने बताया कि इस महीने में अधिकतर छिटपुट बरसात ही देखने को मिलेगी। हालांकि 18 से 22 और 25 से 27 सितंबर के बीच मौसम ज्यादा सक्रिय रहने की संभावना है।
इन अवधियों में गरज-चमक के साथ अच्छी बारिश हो सकती है, जबकि बाकी दिनों में बादल, उमस और हल्की फुहारें बनी रहेंगी। इससे तापमान में गिरावट आएगी लेकिन नमी की वजह से उमस बढ़ेगी।
स्वास्थ्य विभाग का कहना है कि ऐसे मौसम में बीमारियों का खतरा भी बढ़ने का डर बना रहता है। इसीलिए बच्चे से लेकर बूढों तक हर किसी को खास ख्याल रखना चाहिए। डॉक्टरों ने बताया कि ठंडा- गरम और बाहर का तला भुना खाने से बचना चाहिए। साथ ही धूप और बारिश में भीगने से बचाव के हर तरीके अपनाने चाहिए।

Much of the UK is set to feel cooler from Tuesday, as more changeable weather moves in.
Parts of the UK are also likely to see some spells of rain, especially to northern and western parts of the UK.
The rest of the week stays a little unsettled with further spells of rain.
It could turn more settled into next week with temperatures rising above average for some, though heatwave conditions are looking increasingly unlikely.
Tuesday will start off relatively warm and muggy across central and south-eastern areas of England but further north and west it will start to feel a little cooler.
That cooler air will be moving south-east behind a cold front that will also bring a spell of rain across England and Wales for a time.
Fresher north-westerly winds will develop across all areas bringing showers - some heavy - to Scotland, Northern Ireland and more north-western parts of England and Wales.
Maximum temperatures will be around five degrees lower than Monday's values with 17 to 22C across the UK.
This is closer to the average for the time of year.
There will be a drier and brighter interlude on Wednesday, with the rest of the week staying a little unsettled with further spells of rain.
Temperatures will remain around average at 15 to 20C.
It will also start to feel a little chillier overnight with temperatures down to 8-12C - meaning those on early commutes to work or school might need to start donning extra layers.
However, while it might feel more autumnal and the right time to pack away the summer clothes, autumn - particularly September - is a fickle time.
Conditions can change with a simple switch in wind direction and we can go from chillier, autumnal weather to warmer conditions and then back again - all within a day.
By Saturday, a west or south-westerly wind will bring something a little warmer with temperatures returning to above average.
With some signs of high pressure building and the prospect of drier and brighter weather, it might feel pleasantly warm for some, especially in south-eastern areas.
It is still a long way off but temperatures could rise temporarily further into next week.
The signs are, though, that a September heatwave is increasingly less likely.

Electricity Demand Rises in Tamil Nadu Amid Heatwave
Several parts of Tamil Nadu, including Chennai, are facing increased power demand this September as unusually high temperatures continue across the state. The extended summer-like weather has pushed electricity consumption to record levels and has resulted in unscheduled power cuts in some areas.
Tamil Nadu’s power demand has increased to around 20,500 MW, compared with about 16,000–17,000 MW during the same period last year. The sharp rise has created a shortage of more than 3,000 MW, putting additional pressure on the state’s power distribution system.
To manage the shortage, the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) has reportedly purchased an additional 2,000 MW of electricity. Officials are taking steps to meet the growing demand and maintain a stable supply across different parts of the state.
Chennai Sees Sharp Increase in Demand
Chennai has also experienced a major increase in electricity consumption. The city’s demand has reached around 4,200–4,500 MW, compared with its usual demand of approximately 3,500–3,800 MW during this period.
The higher demand has placed additional pressure on the power network. Some residential areas have experienced repeated interruptions, leading to frustration among residents.
Several areas of Chennai, including Madipakkam, Tambaram, Velachery, and Anna Nagar, have reported power-related problems. Residents have also raised concerns about a lack of clear information regarding scheduled maintenance and power restoration
Protests Over Power Cuts
The power disruptions have also resulted in protests in different parts of Tamil Nadu. Residents in areas such as Tirunelveli, Tiruchi, and Ambasamudram reportedly held demonstrations after experiencing power cuts, particularly during the night.
Similar protests were reported in Royapuram and Tiruvallur. In Tiruvallur, residents reportedly blocked a road on September 10 following a prolonged power outage.
In Thandurai village, residents faced electricity disruptions for more than eight hours a day because of cable damage near Paruthipattu. The power supply has since been restored in the area.
Officials Monitor the Situation
TNPDCL officials have said that steps are being taken to maintain a stable electricity supply across the state. In Chennai, senior officials are closely monitoring the power grid and responding to complaints from residents.
The authorities are also working to address technical problems and reduce the impact of unexpected outages. With electricity demand remaining high because of the continued heat, officials are expected to closely monitor consumption and supply levels.
The situation highlights the pressure that extreme and prolonged heat can place on power infrastructure. As temperatures remain high, maintaining a reliable electricity supply will remain a major challenge for Tamil Nadu, particularly in high-demand areas such as Chennai.

They say that education is not limited to the four walls and corners of the classroom, but three elementary schools in Quezon City took that age-old adage further with a real-life lesson in addressing the worsening impacts of climate change.
Diosdado P. Macapagal Elementary School (DPMES), Manuel L. Quezon Elementary School (MLQES), and Placido Del Mundo Elementary School (PDMES) this year have each launched their respective OASIS Schoolyards, multipurpose outdoor spaces where students can play and where some teachers hold class.
These functional schoolyards are built to serve as more than just idyllic backdrops. Given their green designs and clean intentions, they serve as an appropriate, even timely setting for lessons related to nature and climate change.
In fact, as their name implies, the OASIS Schoolyards offer respite from extreme temperatures that either lead to class suspensions or, failing that, put students through the wringer of attending face-to-face classes in discomforting and increasingly dangerous heat index levels.
These outdoor venues are technically not classrooms. Notwithstanding, they already offer a glimpse of what Philippine education can look like if we visualize it outside of the confines of heat-trapping concrete buildings.
Breath of fresh air
Diosdado P. Macapagal Elementary School Assistant Principal Enelda Martinez had the privilege of witnessing the country’s inaugural OASIS Schoolyard in plan and in practice.
Since 2024, she has seen the project develop at the hands of the Temasek Foundation and the Resilient Cities Network — and later, through the collective enterprise of the school’s own community to add some personalized, lasting improvements to the schoolyard.
“Overall, the acceptance is really positive… It is accepted by parents and children alike, since it was their first time seeing something like this. So the impact on them is usually seen in their cooperation,” Martinez said in an interview.
In the beginning, the school parent-teacher association was on the ground helping out with tidying and cleaning up the schoolyard.
The space offers as many possible uses as the imagination can conjure. On top of being a common play area, it has lately served as an outdoor library of sorts for reading, which was noted by the school official as the most common class activity hosted by the schoolyard.
Kindergarteners use it for scheduled playtime, while first-graders lean on it for their reading time.
“They read there to have a change of atmosphere, not just the classroom. So mostly really, they also have access to ways of storytelling,” Martinez said.
As for higher grades, namely intermediate students, the schoolyard is allotted for their MAPEH (Music, Arts, Physical Education, and Health) subject.
In the previous school term, there were designated times for each grade level to use the area due to inevitable space constraints.
“One at a time. For example, if two sections are already down there, the others cannot go to the schoolyard yet. So mostly…they do not use it simultaneously. That way, everyone can take their turn to play,” Martinez said.
According to the assistant principal, the school, out of its own initiative, later added “bahay kubo” or huts to complement and make the project more attractive, with schoolchildren themselves participating in painting these structures.
Maintenance of the schoolyard is likewise straightforward, usually entailing just routine sweeping of fallen leaves, as the children know not to litter. Utility personnel are specifically assigned to clean the area.
“The schoolyard is wonderful because it doesn’t get too hot. You were able to see the trees. There are also bahay kubo that we added… So mostly it all adds to the experience of our school being well-ventilated,” Martinez said.
Divine by design
According to the designer engaged to implement the three pilot OASIS Schoolyards in Quezon City, the challenge of adapting the concept and tailor-fitting it to each of the participating schools starts with tracing it back to its Parisian roots.
Tanata co-founder and principal landscape architect Alfonso Ancheta said the OASIS program started in Paris as an initiative to renovate different public schools that were not necessarily conducive to learning and development.
“That program was then carried by Resilient Cities Network… They looked into what other markets they could kind of implement this type of way of designing. And they saw that Asia was kind of the next place where they could see how to implement this design. And the Philippines was chosen because Quezon City wanted to be part of the network of cities,” Ancheta said in an interview.
To mitigate risks like heat and flooding, the designer’s firm first held workshops with the principals, teachers, and especially the students of each pilot school.
“We had around maybe five workshops before we actually implemented or before we actually started doing design. The idea was to be able to familiarize the students with what disasters can be caused. Also to understand where they’re coming from and if they understand what the different disasters or natural calamities that they face within the year, within their lifetimes,” Ancheta said.
“But for the schoolyard specifically, being that we’re in a tropical country, and being with the number of students that are in Filipino public schools, in Manila specifically, the resilience aspect and the sustainability aspect has to come with materials. So in terms of mitigating heat, the idea was to bring in more greenery to break up,” he added.
The landscape architect explained that DPMES, MLQES, and PDMES had very different archetypes that correspondingly required different ways of mitigating heat.
“DPMES, they have a big quadrangle in the middle. So what we ended up doing is that we cut the quadrangle basically in half and added like this little OASIS center where there are trees, there are plant boxes, there are also terraces so that they can sit, and then they can also use it to play. And if teachers would like, they can also use it as outdoor classrooms. So that’s the idea behind it, you know, breaking up the big chunks of concrete to be able to mitigate the heat a little bit,” Ancheta said.
He pointed out the irony of still using concrete, as noted by many of the Parisian architects who were consulted for the project during the presentation of the design.
“But the idea behind it is that there are 4,000 students in a given school. So the number of people that will go through that, if we use wood or something more natural, it will deteriorate quickly. Plus, it’s also more exposed to the elements. You know, we can’t necessarily put that into the design without the cost ballooning,” Ancheta said.
Fortunately, DPMES was noted to be a “little bit more blessed” in terms of spaces, including a lot of shaded areas that were later retrofitted, with the areas containing the trees made more “conducive” for the community.
For the school’s flood mitigation, the design firm focused on using more porous materials, such as sand and cocoa cubes, as well as helping to fix the drainage system in general.
“Manuel L. Quezon, we kind of implemented the same thing also. They have a big triangle that is pretty much their main thoroughfare for the students. We also implemented terraces. And then we also put big tree planter boxes or tree holes so that we can plant trees to break up, you know, to add shade in that area. The good thing about MLQES is that they also have a nicely shaded area,” Ancheta said.
PDMES, however, was noted to be a “little troublesome” due to budget constraints limiting the scope of what the design firm hoped to achieve.
“Also, there were some renovations that would have been going on after we do the retrofit that might cause some problems with the design that we’ll put. So it might just get destroyed, basically. So we had to pretty much limit the space that we’re using,” Ancheta said.
Form meets function
On a different note, PDMES was where Tanata introduced the more flood mitigation-related processes.
Here, they used gabion walls or benches, which are made up of or the stability is done by getting rocks and loose stones placed in a box and then reinforced with wood.
“That’s where we added the more natural elements. We put wood slats on top. So they can use them as benches. They can use them to run around, jump around. It’s also right beside the volleyball court. So it’s a perfect little set of bleachers for them to watch their friends play volleyball. It’s also right outside of the library. So it also acts like an outdoor library for the students when they want to read a book outside or if they want to do homework closer to the library,” Ancheta said.
Beyond the aspect of heat and flood mitigation, the designer explained that their primary concern was “just getting the students to use the space.”
“Before we did our implementations, the space wasn’t really used as a place to stay in. That was the first thing that we recognized. These spaces were all transient spaces. So they’re literally just spaces that they go through in their day-to-day because they just have to go through it instead of…sitting there, staying with their friends, reading, talking, playing, etc. So the goal was to really bring the, make the space alive,” Ancheta said.
“The flood mitigation and the heat mitigation were always at the back of our minds, right? But then that also came with how we can implement that within the context of building a community for the children as well,” he added.
To further inspire community participation, the firm intentionally left the schoolyards unpainted so that the schoolchildren can be the ones to decorate these themselves.
Room for growth
Nonetheless, the landscape architect acknowledged that not every school will have the same opportunity to create their own iteration of the OASIS Schoolyard or a similar initiative.
“Not all schools have space. In public schools specifically, there was a shortlist of 11 public schools from the whole of Quezon City. And from the 11, there were only six that got into the final round, and three were chosen,” Ancheta said.
“The population of the school very much contributes to how the school handles the space. So if you have more students, most likely things are going to be paved, things are going to be asphalted. So that doesn’t help with the heat. That doesn’t help with the flooding as well because if you have a more natural area, the ground can seep the water better. If you have a more natural space also, the heat won’t get reflected by the road or the cement or the asphalt,” he added.
The designer also contrasted the localization of the OASIS Schoolyards with their Parisian counterparts.
“In Paris, it doesn’t really rain. So that in itself is already something that people have to pretty much consider. In Europe, in general, they have four seasons, right? So they have more hot seasons; they have more temperate seasons. In the Philippines, it’s either you have a warm or dry season, right? So that in itself, your mindset has to shift. I think that’s why a lot of the Parisian architects, when we presented them the designs, were confused because their mandate, their goal was to bring nature back into the space, wherein our goal was the same,” Ancheta said.
“However, the way things are, the situation the Philippines is in specifically… it has to be done in a different way,” he added.
Population was cited as a major factor, with MLQES being approximated to have 6,000 to 8,000 students, whereas schools in Paris only had an estimated 400 students each.
“And even if this space is bigger than the Parisian public schools…just the amount of feet that will go through it will deteriorate more natural spaces quickly, right? So, you know, we had to take that into consideration because we didn’t want, by month six, it’s already destroyed. It’s already something that the kids can’t use anymore. And we saw that, yes, concrete is something that can help. The porous concrete also, something that can help with regard to flood mitigation, right? I guess the concern more there is just more of like the budgetary allotment. Because porous concrete is pretty expensive,” Ancheta said.
“Well, luckily enough for us, I guess during with the three OASIS schools… weren’t really flooded, or they don’t get flooded. They’re in places where it doesn’t necessarily get flooded. So it’s a good thing. I cannot say with regard to the other schools,” he added.
Sky’s the limit
Meanwhile, Quezon City Education Affairs Unit Head Maricris Veloso noted that MLQES recently needed some minor repairs done, namely repainting attributed to the effects of continuous heavy rainfall.
The city official has since confirmed plans to expand the initiative following the launch of the three pilot OASIS Schoolyards.
“We are proposing under the local…through the local school board, under the Special Education Fund, three additional sites just to expand initially. So we’re looking at three schools. Those are Quirino High School, San Bartolome Elementary School, and Ramon Magsaysay Elementary School,” Veloso said in an interview.
She mentioned the availability of space as a main consideration, citing how the implementation of the schoolyards in PDMES and MLQES was different from the scope of that of DPMES.
“You might be surprised… It’s really seeing how we adapt to the available space. So Ramon Magsaysay, especially, has a big land that can be converted. So we want to have more of those types like Diosdado,” Veloso said.
The local government official also noted an online meeting with the three principals of the new target schools, with DPMES sharing their learnings and challenges alike.
“It’s more of how do we ensure that the physical arrangement, design, would be retained, given that we have thousands of students who step on that…area. I think it’s more really of ensuring that we get to maintain this installation,” Veloso said.
“I asked Diosdado. The students are very eager to go to school, to play in the playground… Even the teachers used the area to teach nature, climate… climate change,” she added.
Finally, she celebrated the example set by DPMES, in particular, of not stopping as a mere beneficiary of the OASIS Schoolyards program.
“They expanded through their own initiatives, which is very good,” Veloso said.
According to her, they are set to present the local government unit’s latest OASIS Schoolyards developments to a heat-related seminar in Singapore next week.
If anything, the schoolyards have proved that the Philippines can go far if it takes its hard-learned lessons beyond the classroom.
— With reports from Gabriel Oliva

A heat-blasted plant can look finished, but looks alone don't always tell gardeners whether to discard it. Burned foliage isn't a definitive sign the plant is dead; the clearer answer is often below the soil line and inside the stems.
Here's what to know
In an explainer, Earth.com said survival depends more on living stems and roots than on how bad the leaves look, meaning even a badly desiccated plant can sometimes recover.
Foliage is often the least reliable place to judge first. Under stress, plants may brown or curl leaves to conserve resources, so visible damage can overstate how far decline has gone.
A better check is the stem: gardeners can lightly scratch it and look for damp, green tissue beneath the surface. Branches that still flex suggest life, while ones that snap quickly are a worse sign.
The roots provide the other key clue. Firm, pale roots suggest possible recovery, but black, soft, foul-smelling roots are more consistent with rot.
Ordinary watering can fail because of the potting mix. When it dries out severely, the soil can become hydrophobic and shed water, allowing it to run down the container's sides and out the drainage holes without soaking the root ball.
To counter that, growers may submerge the root ball in room-temperature water for about 30 to 60 minutes so the soil can take up moisture again. After soaking, let the plant drain well, then keep it in the shade.
Earth.com's advice applies to plants dealing with extreme heat and drought stress.
What can be done?
You can take smaller plants out of their pots to soak, while larger ones can be soaked in their containers. In either case, they should not sit in water too long, because waterlogged roots can lose oxygen and begin to rot.
A plant can need days or even weeks to bounce back after a soak.
While waiting, gardeners should avoid full sun, skip fertilizer until new growth shows up, and postpone heavy pruning until the plant has begun to recover. If proper watering has not produced progress after two or three weeks, the next step may be to lift the root ball and inspect the roots.
A 2- to 3-inch mulch layer can reduce evaporation, while watering at the start or end of the day can help more moisture stay in the soil.
Choosing heat-tolerant plants is another smart move.
Not every heat-stressed plant will return, but a quick look at the stems and roots can show whether it is dead or simply holding on. In some cases, a careful soak is enough to turn an apparent loss into a recovery.
Where can I learn more?
The same clues come up in everyday gardens, where extreme heat can leave peppers, cucumbers, and tomatoes looking far gone. These stories show when summer stress is the main issue and when a struggling plant may be facing something else.
• In Georgia, a wilted cowhorn pepper was protecting itself in the heat, not dying.
• In Maryland, tomatoes in 100-degree weather can shut down at the roots before rebounding.
• Summer growers keep leafy greens going by breaking a few gardening rules in hot weather.
That is why a wilted or browned plant is worth checking before you toss it. Heat, root trouble, watering habits, and even disease can produce similar distress signals, even though the fix may be very different.

Himachal weather: Yellow alert issued for 6 districts today
As per the State Emergency Operation Centre, as many as 61 roads remain blocked across Himachal
As many as 61 roads continue to remain blocked across Himachal while about 189 transformers are disrupted as a result of heavy rains during the ongoing monsoon season.
As per the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC), out of the total blocked roads, as many as 28 are in Mandi, 12 in Kullu, 10 in Kangra, four in Shimla, three in Una and two each in Sirmaur and Lahaul and Spiti. Also, as many as 171 transformers are disrupted in Mandi, 17 in Chamba and one in Shimla. Five drinking water supply schemes are also disrupted in Theog in Shimla.
Meanwhile, light to moderate rain is very likely to continue across the state today as the State's Meteorological Centre has issued yellow alerts for six districts. The districts include Kangra, Kullu, Kinnaur, Lahaul and Spiti, Chamba and Sirmour. Light rain is also expected to occur in rest of the state.
